David Calderwood
DAY-vid KAWL-der-wood
proper noun
From the Scots place-name Calderwood (the wood by the Calder water); David from the Hebrew, “beloved.”

Biblical Definition

David Calderwood (1575–1650) was a Scottish minister and the great historian of the Reformed Kirk, whose labour preserved for posterity the record of Scotland’s struggle to keep her church free from prelacy and royal control. A firm opponent of King James’s Five Articles of Perth and of every encroachment of episcopacy upon the Presbyterian order, he was silenced, imprisoned, and driven into exile in Holland, where from that refuge he wrote in defence of the church’s liberties. His monumental True History of the Church of Scotland gathered the acts, letters, and testimonies of the Kirk into a faithful chronicle, that later generations might know how dearly their fathers had bought the freedom of Christ’s house. In an age when kings would rewrite the past to justify their designs, Calderwood counted the faithful recording of God’s dealings a sacred trust. His life preaches that the memory of the church’s sufferings is not to be lost, that God’s providence in preserving His people is to be told to the generations following, and that the historian who fears God will not flatter the powerful but set down the truth. He laboured that the crown rights of the Redeemer, and the cost at which they were maintained, might never be forgotten by the Kirk he loved.

Webster 1828 Definition

Scottish minister and historian of the Kirk, author of the True History of the Church of Scotland.

David Calderwood (1575–1650), Scottish Presbyterian minister and church historian.

A steadfast opponent of the Five Articles of Perth and of episcopacy imposed upon the Kirk.

Silenced, imprisoned, and exiled to Holland for resisting royal control of the church.

Author of the True History of the Church of Scotland, a faithful chronicle of the Reformed Kirk.

Laboured that the sufferings and liberties of the church might be preserved for later generations.

Key Scripture

Psa 78:4 — "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done."

Deu 32:7 — "Remember the days of old, consider the years of many generations: ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee."

Psa 102:18 — "This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD."

Heb 13:7 — "Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation."

Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the sacred duty of recording God’s dealings with His church.

expand to see more

David Calderwood is preserved because the church forgets her own history at her peril. He counted the faithful chronicling of the Kirk’s sufferings and God’s providences a sacred trust, and his labour rebukes an age that neither reads nor remembers how dearly the freedom of Christ’s house was bought.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Calderwood is the faithful remembrance and honest recording of God’s dealings with His people, that the generation to come might know His strength and the cost of fidelity. He wrote history not to flatter kings but to tell the truth, holding that the memory of the church’s witness must be handed down. His exile for the church’s liberties preaches that even the historian may suffer for the crown rights of Christ.

Hebrew Roots

The name is joined to the Kirk’s memory of her own sufferings and the duty of telling them to the generations.

expand to see more

Calderwood’s history roots the Covenanter memory: the Kirk’s liberties were bought with suffering.

His resistance to Perth and prelacy upholds the Presbyterian order recovered at the Reformation.

His exile in Holland links the Scottish and Dutch Reformed sufferers under one cause.

His faithful chronicling obeys the command to shew God’s works to the generation to come.

His refusal to flatter kings shows the God-fearing historian who sets down truth over favour.

Usage

"Calderwood’s True History remains a primary source for the story of the Reformed Kirk."

"He is cited as the great chronicler of Scotland’s struggle against imposed episcopacy."

"His example is invoked whenever the church is charged to remember and record God’s providences."
